newsitem.title: USA: Intel Q2 seen higher but market eyes Q3.
newsitem.headline: Intel Q2 seen higher but market eyes Q3.

text.p: Intel Corp is due to report second quarter results after the market close Tuesday, but analysts will be most heavily focused on the company's expectations for the third quarter.

The world's largest semiconductor manufacturer is expected to report split-adjusted second quarter earnings per share of $0.90, compared with a split-adjusted $0.59 in the year-ago second quarter, according to First Call.

Intel released a second quarter profit warning on May 30, and analysts said they are now more focussed on whether the company can grow revenues sequentially in the third quarter, and to what extent its strong profit margins will be eroded.
"We know that margins are going to go below 60 percent in the third quarter," said Dan Niles, semiconductor analyst at Robertson, Stephens & Co.
The question is whether Intel can hold in the 57-59 percent range or dip further, he said.

"I'm in the school of thought that it gets into the high 50s by Q3 until they get 0.25 (micron manufacturing) really ramped up," he said, referring to Intel's transition to denser, more cost-effective computer chip design.

Gross margin projections are key to how much analysts might adjust their full-year earnings estimates downward, as expected, after the second quarter report. Intel's gross margins soared to 64.2 percent in the first quarter.
The company has said it expects 1997 gross margins as a whole to be 60 percent, "plus or minus a few points;" over the long term it expects 50 percent, "plus or minus a few points."
Intel closed up 1-7/8 Monday at 78-3/4, the first trading day after its two-for-one stock split over the weekend. The company said it would report earnings today on a post-split basis.

Intel is going through what Chief Executive Officer Andrew Grove said last month is a "monumental" product transition, and Wall Street is watching competition building for the first time in years from Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Cyrix Corp, who are also undergoing major product overhauls.

Grove estimates that by the fourth quarter, about 90 percent of Intel's microprocessor revenues will come from its Pentium processors with MMX multimedia technology and from the new Pentium II processors.

Analysts expect the competition to exert downward pressure on the average price Intel charges for its chips. PaineWebber analyst John Lazlo recently cut his average selling price estimate by $6 to $259, saying he expects Intel to cut prices on older Pentium chips more steeply to make way for new products.
Intel said on May 30 second quarter revenues would be five to 10 percent below the $6.4 billion it reported in the first quarter and gross margins would be below first quarter levels.
Second quarter revenues towards the bottom end of this range, of around $5.8 billion, would nevertheless be up 26 percent from the $4.62 it posted in the year-ago period.
"Whatever they report, I think they're going to be fairly cautious about what they say about the third quarter," said David Wu, analyst with ABN AMRO Chicago Corp.

With full year earnings per share estimates ranging from $7 to $11.25 prior to the stock split -- or $3.50 to $5.75 on a post-split basis -- the higher estimates on Wall Street are expected to be trimmed. It's only a question of by how much. "The bottom line is estimates will come down regardless of what they do," said Niles.

But the technology bellwether share could perform well if the company gave guidance that sequential revenue would be flat to up modestly in the third quarter, with gross marrgins in the high 50 percent range, he added.
